bib.title: Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers", Yongchao Zhou, Andrei Ioan Muresanu, Ziwen Han, Keiran Paster, Silviu Pitis, Harris Chan, Jimmy Ba (Toronto / Vector / Waterloo). ICLR 2023 conference paper, arXiv 2211.01910v2 (10 Mar 2023).

COVERAGE: Read all 103,847 of 103,847 chars, pages 1 to 43, including Appendices A to F (task tables, BBII selection, templates, CoT Table 7, cost analysis, generated-instruction tables 8 to 17, additional figures). I skimmed the reference list for origins only.

VERDICT ON THE TARGET NOTE (08-prompt-optimization.md, APE section)
- The trigger "Let's work this out in a step by step way to be sure we have the right answer", with 82.0 vs 78.7 on MultiArith: CONFIRMED. The model was text-davinci-002, zero-shot CoT. Table 7, p22, and Sec 4.3, p7.
- Human triggers ranging from 45.7 to 78.7, and 17.7 with no trigger: CONFIRMED. These are the nine human-designed rows in Table 7: lowest "The answer is after the proof." 45.7, highest "Let's think step by step." 78.7, and "(Zero-shot) 17.7". The human rows come from Kojima et al. 2022, plus templates from Ahn et al. 2022 and Reynolds & McDonell 2021. They are not new APE measurements.
- "Score candidates by log-probability of correct outputs": INACCURATE as a general description of APE. The paper compares two score functions, execution accuracy (0-1 match) and log P(A | [ρ;Q]). It adopts EXECUTION ACCURACY as the default because it correlates better with test accuracy (Sec 5.2). Log-likelihood is the score only in the CoT experiment. There APE picked a "Let's..." prefix that maximised the likelihood of correct reasoning chains, which were first generated with "Let's think step by step." and filtered for correct answers. Suggested fix: "default scoring is execution accuracy on held-out demos; for the CoT trigger, candidates were scored by the likelihood of filtered correct reasoning chains."
- Worth adding: the gain on GSM8K was 40.7 to 43.0. On the 12 Kojima tasks, the APE trigger improved 6 of 12 (Figure 10).

CLAIMS
1. The APE trigger beats "Let's think step by step" on MultiArith and GSM8K.
   number: 78.7 to 82.0 (MultiArith); 40.7 to 43.0 (GSM8K)
   setup: InstructGPT text-davinci-002, zero-shot CoT, answer-prefix search constrained to start with "Let's"
   quote: "This generated prompt further improves performance from 78.7 to 82.0 on MultiArith and from 40.7 to 43.0 on GSM8K."
   where: p7, Sec 4.3 (~char 27,500)
2. The CoT scoring was the likelihood of correct reasoning steps.
   number: none
   setup: same as claim 1
   quote: "we generate a dataset of questions and reasoning steps generated using InstructGPT with “Let’s think step by step.” Then, we remove any data points that had incorrect answers. Finally, we use APE to find a prompt starting with “Let’s” that maximizes the likelihood of these correct reasoning steps."
   where: p7
3. Human trigger range and no-trigger baseline.
   number: 45.7 to 78.7; 17.7
   setup: MultiArith, text-davinci-002, Table 7 (rows 2 to 10 human-designed)
   quote: "10 The answer is after the proof. 45.7 / - (Zero-shot) 17.7" and "2 Human-Designed Let’s think step by step. (*1) 78.7"
   where: p22, Table 7
4. Zero-shot CoT context.
   number: 17.7 to 78.7 (MultiArith); 10.4 to 40.7 (GSM8K)
   setup: Kojima et al.'s result as reported in this paper
   quote: "improves the zero-shot performance of InstructGPT on MultiArith (Roy & Roth, 2016) from 17.7 to 78.7 and improves performance on GSM8K(Cobbe et al., 2021) from 10.4 to 40.7"
   where: p7
5. APE is at least human-level on all 24 Instruction Induction tasks and on 17 of 21 BIG-Bench tasks.
   number: 24/24; 17/21
   setup: Honovich et al. 2022 tasks, executed on InstructGPT (text-davinci-002); BBII is a curated subset of 21 tasks scored on normalized performance
   quote: "better or comparable performance to the instructions generated by human annotators on 24/24 Instruction Induction tasks and 17/21 curated BIG-Bench tasks"
   where: p1, abstract
6. IQM beats humans.
   number: 0.810 vs 0.749
   setup: interquartile mean over 24 tasks, InstructGPT, 5 random seeds
   quote: "APE with InstructGPT outperforms human-engineered prompts, obtaining an IQM of 0.810 vs humans’ 0.749"
   where: p6
7. Setup for Instruction Induction.
   number: 5 demonstrations; 5 seeds
   setup: text-davinci-002
   quote: "For each task, we sample five input-output pairs from the training data and select the best instruction using algorithm 1." and "We repeat our experiments five times with different random seeds"
   where: p5-6
8. The default score is execution accuracy, because it correlates better than log-prob.
   number: 250 instructions per task; 10 test points
   setup: 24 tasks, InstructGPT 175B, forward mode, Spearman correlation
   quote: "We generate 250 instructions per task using InstructGPT (175B) in “forward” mode and compute the metric score and test accuracy on 10 test data points... Figure 7 (Middle) shows that the execution accuracy aligns better with the test performance across the tasks. Thus, we choose it as our default metric"
   where: p9
9. Log-prob was hypothesised to help as a softer signal.
   number: none
   quote: "we consider the log probability of the desired answer given the instruction and question under the target model M, which on a per sample basis, is logP (A | [ρ;Q])."
   where: p5
10. Sample size: returns diminish, human level is reached at 64, and the default is 50.
    number: 4 to 128; 64; 50
    quote: "we increase the sample size from 4 to 128... human-level performance is achieved with 64 instruction samples. Thus, we choose 50 as our default sample size."
    where: p8
11. Iterative Monte Carlo search gives only marginal gains. The paper reports no single gain number; this claim is qualitative.
    number: about 3 rounds before stabilising; 6 tasks compared
    quote: "we observe diminishing returns to further selection rounds as the quality seems to stabilize after three rounds." and "iterative search marginally improves performance on tasks where APE underperforms humans but achieves similar performance on the other tasks." Also: "we use APE without iterative search as default unless otherwise stated."
    where: p5, p9
12. Few-shot: prepending the instruction helps on 21 of 24 tasks, but hurts on Rhymes, Large Animal and Second Letter.
    quote: "adding an instruction achieves a comparable or better test performance than the standard in-context learning performance on 21 of 24 tasks."
    where: p6
13. TruthfulQA: true and informative rises to over 40%, against 30% for the human "help" prompt. Instructions tend to land at the ends of the Pareto frontier.
    setup: 100 training questions out of 817, 717 test, 200 candidates, GPT-judge/GPT-info metrics
    quote: "APE achieves over 40% accuracy in providing both true and informative answers (v.s. 30% by the “help” prompt from humans)"
    where: p8
14. Instructions transfer poorly across models.
    number: none
    quote: "there is a significant performance drop when we use the instructions from InstructGPT to steer the GPT-3 model, and vice versa... the alignment between the scoring model and execution model is crucial"
    where: p23
15. Cost: larger instruction-tuned proposers are cheaper overall, because most of the cost is scoring.
    quote: "the most significant proportion of the cost is scoring with InstructGPT, which scales with the length of instructions generated"
    where: p24, Fig 11
16. Instructions condense context.
    quote: "APE instructions reduce the number of prompt tokens by up to an order of magnitude compared to in-context learning."
    where: p24
17. Reward hacking on Rhymes: selected instructions echo the input word.
    quote: "4 of 5 filtered instructions ask to echo the input word. These proposals effectively hack the evaluation with near-perfect test accuracy, as every word rhymes with itself."
    where: p20, Table 8

LIMITS
- The headline 24/24 result depended on later hyperparameter retuning. The appendix figures come from an older version: "only reached human level on 19 of 24 tasks" (p34, Table 17).
- BBII: APE is worse than humans on 4 of 21 tasks (logical fallacy 24.0 to 12.0; presuppositions 13.0 to 5.5; ruin names 1.3 to -14.7; operators 48.0 to 47.0; Table 6, p21).
- The CoT trigger improved only 6 of 12 reasoning tasks. The authors concede that Shuffled Objects and Last Letter "are hard to optimize on with a general prompt" (Fig 10).
- TruthfulQA results "are not in any way compatible with the original benchmarks" and are "not 'true few-shot learning'" (p7).
- Execution accuracy can be gamed (Rhymes), and instructions overfit the zero-shot setting.
- The meta-prompt template "makes a difference, improving the performance on some tasks while impairing others" (p23).
- Dated: everything runs on 2022 OpenAI models (text-davinci-002, GPT-3 ada to davinci), which are now deprecated. Costs use API rates "as of September 1, 2022". The definition of prompt engineering excludes chaining and tools (footnote 1).

BUILDS ON
- Honovich et al. (2022), instruction induction: the tasks, the "Greedy" baseline and the execution-accuracy metric.
- Kojima et al. (2022), zero-shot CoT.
- Zelikman et al. (2022), STaR: inspired the CoT optimisation.
- Discrete prompt search: Gao et al. (2021), Shin et al. (2020, AutoPrompt), Davison et al. (2019) for scoring, Jiang et al. (2020) and Yuan et al. (2021) for paraphrasing.
- Program synthesis: Gulwani et al. (2017), Ellis et al. (2021).
- Score estimation: Li et al. (2022), Maclaurin & Adams (2015).
- Lin et al. (2022), TruthfulQA. Suzgun et al. (2022), BBH, used for BBII filtering. Agarwal et al. (2021), IQM.

CODE (verbatim, Table 5, p19)
- Forward generation: "I gave a friend an instruction and five inputs. The friend read the instruction and wrote an output for every one of the inputs.\nHere are the input-output pairs: ... The instruction was<COMPLETE>"
- Resample: "Generate a variation of the following instruction while keeping the semantic meaning.\nInput: [INSTRUCTION]\nOutput:<COMPLETE>"
- Zero-shot-CoT: "Instruction: Answer the following question.\nQ: [INPUT]\nA: Let's <INSERT>. [OUTPUT]"
- Algorithm 1 (p4): propose U, then loop: score on a random subset, keep the top k%, keep or resample; finally return the arg max on the full Dtrain.
- Repo: https://github.com/keirp/automatic_prompt_engineer

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p2): the APE workflow diagram (propose, score, keep or discard, resample) plus the IQM bar chart against the human line. It shows the whole loop in one picture.
- Fig 7 (p9): left is sample size vs accuracy (diminishing returns); middle is Spearman correlation of log-prob vs execution accuracy; right is APE vs iterative APE. It covers three ablations at a glance.
- Fig 6 (p9): survival curves by model size and by iteration round. They show proposal quality visually.
- Table 7 (p22): the CoT trigger ranking. This is the best candidate for the note's MultiArith claim.
- Fig 5 (p8): the TruthfulQA true/informative frontier.

PROBLEMS
- Extraction was clean. Figure-embedded numbers (Fig 1b bars) come out as loose tokens, and I did not quote them.
- Typos in the source: "Demostration", "text-davanci-002", "exiting templates".
- I found no embedded instructions.
